nicheStories.title: Pro-Israel hawks lash out after most House Dems vote to cut aid
nicheStories.description: Public opinion on Israel is shifting rapidly, but there was little evidence of that at a House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing Wednesday. The Middle East and North Africa Subcommittee's discussion of "The Next Phase of the Abraham Accords" largely reflected a Washington consensus on Israel that is quickly losing support.The discussion was ostensibly focused on expanding the agreements, signed during President Donald Trump’s first term, that normalized relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Morocco. But the conversation quickly expanded to broader questions of the U.S.-Israel and Israel-Palestine relationship. In particular, lawmakers and witnesses explored whether the pursuit of a Palestinian state was a necessary step to further the accords and bring in Saudi Arabia, which has previously said they would not sign the accords without a pathway to statehood. Four of the five Democratic members present – Reps. Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.), and Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) — were among the narrow minority of the party who voted against an amendment to cut off aid to Israel. The one exception to this was Rep. Bill Keating (D-Mass.), who was among the 19 AIPAC-supported Democrats later “punished” by the lobby group as a result of their support for the amendment, according to the New York Times.The witness panel skewed the same direction. David Friedman, President Donald Trump's first-term ambassador to Israel, has previously called for "Israeli sovereignty over the entirety of Judea and Samaria" — the biblical name for the West Bank favored by the Israeli right. Asher Fredman testified as executive director of the Misgav Institute, a think tank that, in October 2023, called for the "relocation and final settlement of the entire Gaza population," according to a translation reported by Mondoweiss. The third witness — Daniel Shapiro, U.S. ambassador to Israel under President Barack Obama — offered the panel's closest thing to a dissenting voice.Shapiro argued that the biggest impediment to peace was the ongoing war in Iran, which he said would result in either “leaving our regional partners to contend with an emboldened Iran” or “a highly costly forever war with massive sustained U.S. military presence,” neither of which would be conducive to regional integration. For the other panelists, however, blame fell squarely on Palestinians' rejection of peace. “The United States should have no role, no role in putting its imprimatur on a corrupt Palestinian state,” Friedman said during his opening remarks. He later said that, in his analysis, Tel Aviv would welcome normalization with Riyadh, but not at the cost of a Palestinian state, which Friedman said was akin to “suicide” for Israelis. The staunchly pro-Israel voices on the panel certainly sensed that the political winds were shifting against Israel, and argued these dynamics would block an expansion of the Abraham Accords. Friedman argued that no Arab country would choose to “make a deal with Trump for two years” and then enter a more unpredictable political landscape. “We'll have to relitigate everything all over again,” he lamented. “We have to take this issue and make it a bipartisan, predictable issue, and that I think will bring a lot of good, a lot of good outcomes.” Speaking directly about the recent vote to cut aid, Friedman added that “If Arab countries think that Israel is losing American support, throw the accords out the window.” Fredman of Misgav, for his part, made the case that there is currently no viable Palestinian partner for peace, citing polling that 53% of Palestinians viewed the October 7 attack favorably and that Hamas remains more popular than rival factions. The strongest point of friction between the Democratic members present and the witnesses was over the issue of settler violence in the West Bank. Sherman pressed on rising attacks, citing Israeli military figures showing a 27% increase and reports of severe attacks up 50%. Friedman waved off the framing entirely. Settler violence, he said, is a "man bites dog" story – because “it doesn't happen that often. But it's so prone with emotion and anger that it gets the headlines."

nicheStories.title: As war drags on, Ukraine’s population is collapsing
nicheStories.description: As the war in Ukraine trudges through its fifth year, deaths there now outnumber births at a nearly four-to-one ratio.According to figures published by the Ukrainian Ministry of Justice this week, Ukraine recorded 73,292 births and 259,853 deaths in the first half of 2026.Ukraine thus records about 12,000 births per month, a sharp drop from the approximately 23,000 births per month it recorded before the war began.Birth rates were notably low in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, which is located at the war’s front line and is now mostly occupied by Russia. Only 134 births were recorded there during the first half of 2026.“Few people are willing to bring children into the world while the country remains at war,” Marta Havryshko, a scholar who focuses on the Russo-Ukraine war, wrote on X. “Every additional year of fighting deepens the demographic crisis and pushes Ukraine closer to becoming an empty land.”In addition, the war has sent millions of Ukrainians abroad.“I don't think it's likely that Europe or other supporters of Ukraine can muster the kind of massive financial investment in a post-war reconstruction […] that would allow millions of Ukrainians to go back home,” Quincy Institute non-resident fellow Almut Rochowanski told RS.“Ukrainian refugees abroad would need to know that they're going home to functioning housing, schools, hospitals and sufficient incomes,” Rochowanski said. “That is a tall order.”The new population figures come as fewer Ukrainians are demonstrating a desire to fight. Earlier this month, anti-conscription protests rocked the western city of Lviv. Ukraine also has about two million draft-dodgers and about 200,000 military deserters, according to the country’s former defense minister.In line with polling it conducted last year, Gallup found last month that Ukrainians’ support for continued fighting remains low. Only 24% of respondents told Gallup that Ukraine should keep fighting until it wins the war. In contrast, 66% wanted a negotiated solution to end it as soon as possible.About 52 million people lived in Ukraine in 1991. Back in May, Denys Uliutin, Ukraine’s Minister of Social Policy, said the country now only has about 22 to 25 million residents.

nicheStories.title: James Woolsey, influential neocon and Iraq War booster, dies at 84
nicheStories.description: R. James “Jim” Woolsey, a major Iraq and GWOT promoter and neoconservative Democrat, passed away Tuesday at 84.Woolsey served briefly as CIA director but rose to much greater prominence as a consistent promoter on television and in the Wall Street Journal’s op-ed pages of both the Iraq War and the broader Global War on Terror, which he sometimes referred to as “World War IV.” Indeed, immediately after the 9/11 attacks, Woolsey was ubiquitous in arguing that Iraqi President Saddam Hussein not only was linked to al-Qaeda but may very well have approved or helped plan the plot himself.After being forced out of his CIA director role by President Bill Clinton in 1994, Woolsey moved increasingly to the right, as noted in a generally respectful obituary published by the New York Times Wednesday, joining with the Washington-based Likudist neoconservatives led by the “Dark Prince” himself, Richard Perle of the American Enterprise Institute (AEI).Woolsey, an engaging if rather glib speaker who never seemed to run out of words, became a key part of what George Mason University anthropologist Janine Wedel identified as the “Neocon Core” in the years running up to and following the Iraq War and the GWOT. That included the promotion of confrontation with Syria and Iran as well as other states deemed hostile to Israel, and, hence, in their view, to the United States, as well.That 11-member core, according to Wedel, included men who would hold key posts under President George W. Bush, among them Bush’s future deputy defense secretary Paul Wolfowitz; his undersecretary of defense, Douglas Feith; his director for Near East policy on the National Security Council, Elliott Abrams; and Vice President Dick Cheney’s chief of staff and national security adviser, I. Lewis “Scooter” Libby.All of these men served on a variety of overlapping boards of major Washington-based organizations and think tanks that aligned themselves with Israel’s right-wing Likud Party. Together, these groups acted as a remarkably effective media echo chamber after 9/11 and in the run-up to the Iraq invasion, particularly in spreading mis- or disinformation about Saddam’s alleged development of nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction programs and ties to al-Qaeda.In addition to Perle and the rest of AEI’s foreign policy wing staff, they included groups such as the Jewish Institute for National Security Affairs (recently renamed the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, or JINSA); the Center for Security Policy (CSP); the more moderate Washington Institute for Near East Policy (WINEP), a spin-off of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee; and the Project for the New American Century (PNAC), a letterhead organization that promoted U.S. global hegemony and regime change in Middle Eastern countries considered hostile to Israel.Woolsey was involved in nearly all of the veritable galaxy of neoconservative front groups created to advocate for policies like invading Iraq. He held positions on the advisory and other boards of CSP, WINEP, and the Committee for the Liberation of Iraq. He also served as the chair of the Leadership Council of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), which, for most of the past 20 years, effectively replaced AEI as the most prominent pro-Israel Washington think tank promoting war with Iran. Woolsey was also a co-founder of United Against a Nuclear Iran (UANI), an advocacy group closely tied to Israeli intelligence that has promoted comprehensive economic sanctions against Tehran since its founding in 2008.Although Woolsey was not a signatory of PNAC’s 1997 charter, which was signed by a number of top Bush Jr. policymakers, including Cheney and Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, he did sign on to nine of the group’s open letters, including an April 2002 statement that called for the administration “to accelerate plans for removing Saddam Hussein from power” and asserted that “Israel’s fight against terrorism is our fight.”Woolsey also served as a member of the Pentagon’s Defense Policy Board, a civilian advisory body during the Bush administration initially chaired and organized by Perle. Just days after 9/11, Perle convened the Board and invited Ahmed Chalabi, head of the previously CIA-backed opposition Iraqi National Congress (INC) and a long-time Perle collaborator, to participate in its deliberations about Iraq as a possible target for U.S. military action and regime change. As a result of that meeting, Wolfowitz dispatched Woolsey — who, like Perle, had already declared on network television news that Hussein was likely to have been behind the attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon — to gather evidence about Saddam’s alleged (but non-existent) ties to al-Qaeda and a previous 1993 bombing in the parking garage of the World Trade Center. His mission — about which neither the State Department nor the CIA (which had several years before severed ties with Chalabi due to their assessment that he was completely unreliable) were informed — ended without acquiring the desired intelligence. Still, Woolsey, backed by the administration and the neoconservative network and echo chamber of which he had become an important part, continued to claim that Saddam and al-Qaeda worked together. Chalabi’s INC nonetheless became the key source of disinformation about Iraq’s alleged weapons of mass destruction that was seized upon and promoted to the mass media by the Pentagon, the White House, and the neoconservative echo chamber, including Woolsey himself.
